extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, historians/philosophers of mathematics, and general readers interested in mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Describing how mathematics is practiced, supported, evaluated, and transmitted — including tools, community structure, epistemic standards (proof/rigor), and expectations for training and specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for recording and duplication tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics requires instruments of writing or recording and of duplication; before printing there were 'scribe factories' for replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain durable, duplicable records of mathematical work (notes, manuscripts, printed copies). Anti-pattern: treating mathematics as purely oral or ephemeral; lack of records inhibits transmission and collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler-and-compass as defining tools of Euclidean geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidean geometry can be defined as the science of ruler-and-compass constructions — the ruler and compass are built into the axioms at the foundation of Euclidean geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in Euclidean geometry, constructions and reasoning consistent with ruler-and-compass methods are the normative standard. Use of other instruments changes the foundational setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of auxiliary tools (abacus, slide rule, computer, physical models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic and applied mathematics have been aided by instruments such as the abacus, the slide rule, and the electronic computer; in some cases physical models are more efficient than computer graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the tool that best serves the problem: use computers for heavy numerical or symbolic tasks; prefer physical scaled models when they offer clearer insight or efficiency. Anti-pattern: defaulting to a single tool (e.g., always using computer graphics) when a model or simpler instrument would be better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating computer-generated images as mathematical constructs, not physical realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer graphics can depict 'objects' that look photographic but have no real-world existence; such images are mathematical or programmatic constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret computer visualizations as representations of mathematical definitions/algorithms; avoid conflating visual realism with physical existence. Verify mathematical properties analytically rather than relying solely on renderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational relevance as a driver of research direction
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability of computers affects mathematics by luring mathematicians toward constructive and algorithmic results and away from purely existential or dialectical results that lack computational meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing problems or methods, consider computational/algorithmic tractability if engagement with computing resources or applications is desired. Note that change in tooling can bias research agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation for Ph.D. candidate background (breadth/depth guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical Ph.D. candidate takes about fourteen to eighteen undergraduate and sixteen graduate courses; estimating one book per course (and doubling for collateral reading) yields about sixty to eighty volumes — roughly two shelves of books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ~60–80 core volumes as a pragmatic target for foundational reading for doctoral preparation. Anti-pattern: trying to master the entire discipline rather than focusing on the two-shelf depth for one’s specialty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist basic-knowledge heuristic (two-foot bookshelf)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given subspecialty, a basic education can be represented by a two-foot bookshelf (about 60 books); extrapolating across mathematics implies many distinct subspecialties (coarse estimate ~1,000; finer classifications >3,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define reasonable, bounded foundational reading lists for specialists; acknowledge that no one can master all areas and plan training accordingly. Use the two-foot bookshelf as a planning heuristic for curricula and self-study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sources of new mathematical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two inexhaustible sources of new mathematical questions: (1) the development of science and technology, which makes new demands on mathematics, and (2) mathematics itself, where completed results spawn new investigations and interconnections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking fruitful research directions, consider problems arising from scientific/technological applications and opportunities to connect apparently unrelated mathematical specialties. Anti-pattern: assuming isolated, purely internal problems are the only source of valuable new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that areas can become internally exhausted
rubrics_metrics.description: Many areas show signs of internal exhaustion (e.g., elementary circle/triangle geometry, classical complex function theory) and may no longer produce strikingly new results within their bounded confines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when choosing problems in historically saturated areas; seek new perspectives, applications, or connections to rejuvenate them. Accept that some fields may be more suitable for pedagogical exercises than for frontier research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ulam's dilemma — limitations on cross-field evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: With an enormous production of theorems annually, no single person can survey all important results; there are effectively no stated criteria that permit evaluation of work across widely separated fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on synthesized judgments from committees of specialists for cross-field decisions; expect value judgments to be narrow, contingent, and often made 'by the market' (refereeing, proposal volume) rather than by global principled criteria. Anti-pattern: presuming universal standards of 'importance' that apply equally across disparate subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criterion for funding/publication decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, federal funding and publication decisions are made by favorable refereeing and by the volume of proposals/papers in an area; panels often allocate quotas to areas and follow a political principle of nonaggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For successful proposals/papers, secure strong favorable peer reviews within your field and be aware that disciplinary representation and committee norms influence outcomes. Anti-pattern: expecting external arbiters to objectively rank disparate fields without reliance on community refereeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value judgments grounded in conception of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of what is valuable in mathematics is based on one's notion of the nature and purpose of mathematics (epistemology/ontology); absent shared criteria, evaluative practices reflect differing fundamental beliefs about mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justifying the importance of work, make explicit underlying conceptions (e.g., emphasis on rigor, applicability, constructiveness) to help communicate value to peers and funders. Anti-pattern: presenting work without articulating its epistemic or practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of apprenticeship and specialist initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding and participating in a mathematical specialty typically requires an arduous apprenticeship of several years; many objects and concepts are unintelligible without this initiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design training paths that provide deep apprenticeship in chosen specialties; set realistic expectations about the time required for comprehension and contribution. Anti-pattern: undervaluing the learning curve and expecting rapid mastery without sustained guided practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity and success markers of the mathematician
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ideal mathematician' is identified by field label, publication output, whose work he uses, and whose taste he follows; he rests his faith on rigorous proof and judges success by discovering new facts about his objects of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate clear scholarly identity (specialty, publication record, intellectual lineage) and prioritize rigorous arguments and novel results as measures of professional success. Recognize the tension between the ideal of rigor and the fuzziness of operational practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical understanding requires contextual immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand mathematics of an earlier period requires penetrating the contemporary individual and collective consciousness; printed records alone rarely capture the full network of meanings and motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians and interpreters should seek contextual evidence (pedagogy, instruments, social practice) beyond texts to reconstruct the intent and meaning of past mathematics. Anti-pattern: treating historical mathematical texts as self-contained expositions of their period's practice.
